claim: PDB is a post-embryonic cholinergic motor neuron derived from the P12 neuroectoblast cell.
source: PDB is a post-embryonic cholinergic motor neuron derived from the P12 neuroectoblast cell (Sulston and Horvitz, 1977), and its cell body resides in the preanal ganglion.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sulston and Horvitz, 1977.

claim: The PDB cell body resides in the preanal ganglion.
source: PDB is a post-embryonic cholinergic motor neuron derived from the P12 neuroectoblast cell (Sulston and Horvitz, 1977), and its cell body resides in the preanal ganglion.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text and is established knowledge about PDB anatomy.

claim: In hermaphrodites, PDB sends a single neurite posteriorly toward the tail tip region, where it makes a sharp 'V-shape' turn to join the dorsal nerve cord to form en passant synapses onto dorsal body wall muscles.
source: In hermaphrodites, PDB sends a single neurite posteriorly toward the tail tip region, where it makes a sharp 'V-shape' turn to join the dorsal nerve cord to form en passant synapses onto dorsal body wall muscles (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A which shows the PDB structure.

claim: PDB plays a role in motor coordination.
source: While the function of PDB has not been extensively studied, a recent study combining mathematical modeling and a cell ablation experiment revealed the role of PDB in motor coordination (Yan et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yan et al., 2017.

claim: The PDB neuron has a unique transient 'H-shape' structure at L2 stage with two posterior neurites (one dorsal neurite and one ventral neurite).
source: Interestingly, we observed that the PDB neuron has a unique transient structure at L2 stage: the ventral neurite sends a tiny commissure to the dorsal side of the worm where it bifurcates to extend one neurite posteriorly and one anteriorly (Figure 1C: upper panels). The PDB neuron therefore often has 'H-shape' structure with two posterior neurites (one dorsal neurite and one ventral neurite) at the early L2 stage (Figure 1C and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 1C and E.

claim: Most PDB neurons at L3/L4 stage contain no posterior neurite.
source: In sharp contrast, the PDB neuron of most L3/L4 animals contained no posterior neurite (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: 82.6% (57/69) of the posterior neurites observed at the L2 stage were pruned within 24 hr.
source: In total, 82.6% (57/69) of the neurites we observed at the L2 stage were pruned within 24 hr.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from tracking individual animals over time.

claim: The posterior neurites are pruned by retraction rather than severing followed by degradation.
source: To distinguish which mechanism the PDB neuron utilizes to prune its posterior neurites, we conducted time-lapse imaging during posterior neurite pruning and found that the posterior neurite became shorter over the development while the dorsal anterior neurite kept growing (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). This indicates that the posterior neurites are pruned by retraction rather than the severing followed by degradation.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: PDB neurite pruning is not dependent on neuronal activity.
source: To determine if PDB pruning is dependent on neuronal activity, we examined mutants of unc-13, which is required for synaptic vesicle fusion and neurotransmitter release (Richmond et al., 1999). At L2 stage of unc-13 animals, we observed PDB posterior neurites at a similar frequency as wildtype, while most of the unc-13 animals at late larval stage (L3-L4) did not have PDB posterior neurites as observed in wildtype (Figure 1B). Consistently, we did not observe significant structural defects in PDB of unc-13 mutants at L4 stage (Figure 2D), suggesting that the PDB neurite pruning is not dependent on the neuronal activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from unc-13 mutants shown in Figures 1B and 2D.

claim: unc-13 is required for synaptic vesicle fusion and neurotransmitter release.
source: To determine if PDB pruning is dependent on neuronal activity, we examined mutants of unc-13, which is required for synaptic vesicle fusion and neurotransmitter release (Richmond et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Richmond et al., 1999.

claim: The V-shape turn of the PDB neurite is achieved by the asymmetric pruning of the posterior but not the anterior neurites at the turning point during PDB development.
source: Taken together, our observation indicates that the V-shape turn of the PDB neurite is achieved by the asymmetric pruning of the posterior but not the anterior neurites at the turning point during PDB development (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental observations presented in the study and illustrated in Figure 1E.

claim: lin-44/wnt is expressed in the hypodermal cells at the tail tip region.
source: Previous works have shown that lin-44/wnt is expressed in the hypodermal cells at the tail tip region (Figure 2A), where it locally inhibits neurite outgrowth and synapse formation, as well as controls neuronal polarity and asymmetric cell division (Herman et al., 1995; Hilliard and Bargmann, 2006; Klassen and Shen, 2007; Maro et al., 2009; Zheng et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by previous work cited and confirmed by Figure 2A in this study.

claim: lin-44 locally inhibits neurite outgrowth and synapse formation, as well as controls neuronal polarity and asymmetric cell division.
source: Previous works have shown that lin-44/wnt is expressed in the hypodermal cells at the tail tip region (Figure 2A), where it locally inhibits neurite outgrowth and synapse formation, as well as controls neuronal polarity and asymmetric cell division (Herman et al., 1995; Hilliard and Bargmann, 2006; Klassen and Shen, 2007; Maro et al., 2009; Zheng et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: At the L2 stage when PDB posterior neurites undergo pruning, the pruning posterior neurite was located in close proximity to the most posterior hypodermal cell, hyp10.
source: Strikingly, at the L2 stage when PDB posterior neurites undergo pruning, we found that the pruning posterior neurite was located in close proximity to the most posterior hypodermal cell, hyp10 (Figure 2B–B' and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2B-B' and C.

claim: hyp10 often showed the brightest BFP expression among the lin-44-expressing cells at the L2 stage.
source: Interestingly, we noticed that hyp10 often showed the brightest BFP expression among the lin-44-expressing cells at the L2 stage.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from imaging experiments.

claim: 54.3% (38/70) of lin-44 mutant animals with no obvious cell fate or guidance defects showed ectopic posterior neurites in PDB at the L4 stage.
source: Among the lin-44 mutant animals with no obvious cell fate or guidance defects, 54.3% (38/70) of them showed ectopic posterior neurites in PDB at the L4 stage, suggesting the defective neurite pruning during PDB development (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Only 30% (15/50) of the posterior neurites observed at the L2 stage animals are pruned by L4 stage in the lin-44 mutants.
source: As expected, we indeed observed that only 30% (15/50) of the posterior neurites observed at the L2 stage animals are pruned by L4 stage in the lin-44 mutants, which is significantly lower than those observed in wildtype (82.6%) (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: lin-44/wnt is required for the pruning of the posterior neurites during PDB development.
source: This result strongly suggests that lin-44/wnt is required for the pruning of the posterior neurites during PDB development.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing pruning defects in lin-44 mutants.

claim: LIN-44/Wnt utilizes LIN-17/Frizzled(Fz) as a primary receptor in many contexts.
source: LIN-44/Wnt utilizes LIN-17/Frizzled(Fz) as a primary receptor in many contexts (Hilliard and Bargmann, 2006; Klassen and Shen, 2007; Sawa et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Only 17.0% of the posterior neurites (9/53) were pruned 24 hr after L2 stage in lin-17(n671) null mutants.
source: While lin-17(n671) null mutants showed significantly more severe cell fate or guidance defects than lin-44/wnt mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), we observed similar posterior neurite pruning defects as lin-44 mutants: only 17.0% of the posterior neurites (9/53) were pruned 24 hr after L2 stage (Figure 3B–3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3B-3D.

claim: The pruning defect in the lin-44; lin-17 double mutants (14.3%: 6/42 of the posterior neurites were pruned) was not significantly different from lin-17 single mutants.
source: The pruning defect in the lin-44; lin-17 double mutants (14.3%: 6/42 of the posterior neurites were pruned) was not significantly different from lin-17 single mutants, suggesting that lin-44 and lin-17 act in the same genetic pathway (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: lin-44 and lin-17 act in the same genetic pathway.
source: The pruning defect in the lin-44; lin-17 double mutants (14.3%: 6/42 of the posterior neurites were pruned) was not significantly different from lin-17 single mutants, suggesting that lin-44 and lin-17 act in the same genetic pathway (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the lack of additive effects in double mutants.

claim: Expression of lin-17 cDNA either from the pan-neuronal promoter (Prgef-1) or the PDB promoter (Pkal-1) significantly rescued the pruning defects of lin-17 mutants.
source: Expression of lin-17 cDNA either from the pan-neuronal promoter (Prgef-1) or the PDB promoter (Pkal-1) significantly rescued the pruning defects of lin-17 mutants, suggesting that lin-17 acts cell-autonomously in PDB (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: lin-17 acts cell-autonomously in PDB.
source: Expression of lin-17 cDNA either from the pan-neuronal promoter (Prgef-1) or the PDB promoter (Pkal-1) significantly rescued the pruning defects of lin-17 mutants, suggesting that lin-17 acts cell-autonomously in PDB (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on cell-specific rescue experiments.

claim: LIN-17/Fz is a receptor that functions in PDB to receive LIN-44/Wnt signal to induce neurite pruning.
source: These results indicate that LIN-17/Fz is a receptor that functions in PDB to receive LIN-44/Wnt signal to induce neurite pruning.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on genetic and rescue experiments.

claim: egl-20/wnt is expressed in the cells around preanal ganglions.
source: In order to distinguish these two possibilities, we conducted the rescue experiment by expressing LIN-44 ectopically using the promoter of another wnt gene, egl-20. egl-20/wnt is expressed in the cells around preanal ganglions (Whangbo and Kenyon, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Whangbo and Kenyon, 1999.

claim: Pegl-20::lin-44 transgenes did not rescue pruning defects of lin-44 null mutants.
source: We found that Pegl-20::lin-44 transgenes did not rescue pruning defects of lin-44 null mutants (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Ectopic anterior expression of lin-44 from the dorsal body wall muscles using the truncated unc-129 promoter (Punc-129dm) was not sufficient to rescue the PDB pruning defect in lin-44 null mutants.
source: Similarly, ectopic anterior expression of lin-44 from the dorsal body wall muscles using the truncated unc-129 promoter (Punc-129dm) (Colavita et al., 1998) was not sufficient to rescue the PDB pruning defect in lin-44 null mutants (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and B, with citation to Colavita et al., 1998 for the promoter.

claim: The transgenes expressing lin-44 from the lin-44 promoter (Ex[Plin-44::lin-44]) completely rescued the pruning defects to the wildtype level.
source: On the other hand, the transgenes expressing lin-44 from the lin-44 promoter (Ex[Plin-44::lin-44]) completely rescued the pruning defects to the wildtype level (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: lin-44/wnt is an instructive cue for the posterior neurite pruning in PDB.
source: This result suggests that lin-44/wnt is an instructive cue for the posterior neurite pruning in PDB.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the ectopic expression experiments showing that lin-44 must be expressed in the correct location to rescue pruning defects.

claim: egl-20/wnt often acts cooperatively and redundantly with lin-44/wnt in various developmental events.
source: egl-20/wnt often acts cooperatively and redundantly with lin-44/wnt in various developmental events (Mizumoto and Shen, 2013; Yamamoto et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The expression of egl-20 under the lin-44 promoter did not rescue the PDB neurite pruning defects of the lin-44 null mutant animals.
source: Interestingly, the expression of egl-20 under the lin-44 promoter did not rescue the PDB neurite pruning defects of the lin-44 null mutant animals, suggesting the functional divergence between lin-44 and egl-20 in neurite pruning (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: There is functional divergence between lin-44 and egl-20 in neurite pruning.
source: Interestingly, the expression of egl-20 under the lin-44 promoter did not rescue the PDB neurite pruning defects of the lin-44 null mutant animals, suggesting the functional divergence between lin-44 and egl-20 in neurite pruning (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the inability of egl-20 to substitute for lin-44 function.

claim: PDB structure is largely unaffected in the mutants of egl-20(n585) and its receptors mig-1/fz and cam-1/Ror.
source: Consistently, PDB structure is largely unaffected in the mutants of egl-20(n585) and its receptors mig-1/fz and cam-1/Ror (Figure 2D and data not shown) (Eisenmann, 2005; Mizumoto and Shen, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D and citations to previous work.

claim: cwn-1 is expressed in the posterior region of the worm.
source: Another Wnt gene, cwn-1, is also expressed in the posterior region of the worm (Harterink et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Harterink et al., 2011.

claim: The PDB morphology was indistinguishable from wildtype in the cwn-1 mutants.
source: The PDB morphology was indistinguishable from wildtype in the cwn-1 mutants (Figure 2D and data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: LIN-44 is the major instructive cue for PDB neurite pruning.
source: While we do not completely exclude the involvement of other Wnts, our results indicate that LIN-44 is the major instructive cue for PDB neurite pruning.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental results showing that other Wnts do not have significant effects on PDB pruning.

claim: Gradient distribution of LIN-44 and EGL-20 plays critical roles in C. elegans development.
source: Genetic experiments such as ectopic expression or overexpression of Wnts, and direct visualization of the Wnt protein have revealed the critical roles of gradient distribution of LIN-44 and EGL-20 in C. elegans (Coudreuse et al., 2006; Klassen and Shen, 2007; Maro et al., 2009; Mizumoto and Shen, 2013; Pani and Goldstein, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Anterior expression of lin-44 from the egl-20 promoter did not induce ectopic pruning of the anterior neurite.
source: First, we did not observe ectopic pruning of the anterior neurite when lin-44/wnt was expressed anteriorly from the egl-20 promoter (data not shown), suggesting that anterior expression of lin-44 is not sufficient to induce anterior neurite pruning in PDB.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations (data not shown).

claim: Anterior expression of lin-44 is not sufficient to induce anterior neurite pruning in PDB.
source: First, we did not observe ectopic pruning of the anterior neurite when lin-44/wnt was expressed anteriorly from the egl-20 promoter (data not shown), suggesting that anterior expression of lin-44 is not sufficient to induce anterior neurite pruning in PDB.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental observation.

claim: During PDB development, both growing anterior and pruning posterior neurites are located close to the lin-44-expressing hyp10 cell.
source: Second, during PDB development, both growing anterior and pruning posterior neurites are located close to the lin-44-expressing hyp10 cell (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The GFP signal from the PDB posterior neurite tip overlaps with the BFP signal from hyp10 while there is a gap between the anterior neurite tip and hyp10.
source: Furthermore, a close examination of the spatial relationship between PDB neurites and the lin-44-expressing cells suggests that the GFP signal from the PDB posterior neurite tip overlaps with the BFP signal from hyp10 while there is a gap between the anterior neurite tip and hyp10 (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is based on detailed examination of imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The fusion construct of the type-II transmembrane protein Neurotactin (Nrt) and Wingless/Wnt (Nrt-Wg) is used to characterize the gradient-independent role of Wingless/Wnt in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, the fusion construct of the type-II transmembrane protein Neurotactin (Nrt) and Wingless/Wnt (Nrt-Wg) is used to characterize the gradient-independent role of Wingless/Wnt (Alexandre et al., 2014; Baena-Lopez et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The mutant fly in which endogenous Wg was replaced with Nrt-Wg was viable with no major morphological defects.
source: Importantly, the mutant fly in which endogenous Wg was replaced with Nrt-Wg was viable with no major morphological defects (Alexandre et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Alexandre et al., 2014.

claim: The Nrt-Wg largely abrogated the gradient distribution of Wingless.
source: They also showed that the Nrt-Wg largely abrogated the gradient distribution of Wingless.
evidence: The claim is based on previous work (implied from context to be Alexandre et al., 2014).

claim: The gradient distribution of Wnt is not essential for normal development in Drosophila.
source: These observations suggest that the gradient distribution of Wnt is not essential for normal development.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the viability of Nrt-Wg flies.

claim: NRT-BFP-LIN-44 fusion proteins are localized on the surface of the lin-44-expressing cells.
source: The BFP signal was observed on the membrane of the tail hypodermal cells including hyp10, suggesting that NRT-BFP-LIN-44 fusion proteins are localized on the surface of the lin-44-expressing cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is based on imaging data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Significant proportions of the nrt-bfp-lin-44 animals have normal PDB structures with no posterior neurites at the L4 stage.
source: Interestingly, we observed significant proportions of the nrt-bfp-lin-44 animals have normal PDB structures with no posterior neurites at the L4 stage (Figure 2D and data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Normal pruning of the posterior neurites was observed in nrt-bfp-lin-44 animals (71.2%, 37/52) comparable to wildtype.
source: Specifically, unlike lin-44 null mutants, we observed normal pruning of the posterior neurites in nrt-bfp-lin-44 animals (71.2%, 37/52) comparable to wildtype (Figure 5C–5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5C-5E.

claim: The membrane-tethered LIN-44 is sufficient to induce normal neurite pruning in PDB.
source: This indicates that the membrane-tethered LIN-44 is sufficient to induce normal neurite pruning in PDB.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data from nrt-bfp-lin-44 animals.

claim: Wnt can be transported via cytonemes and extracellular vesicles (EVs).
source: In addition to the traditional model of Wnt gradient formation by simple secretion and chemical diffusion, recent works have started to reveal the alternative modes of Wnt transport via cytonemes and extracellular vesicles (EVs) (Gross et al., 2012; Routledge and Scholpp, 2019; Saha et al., 2016; Stanganello et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to recent work.

claim: The DA9 neuron is a cholinergic motor neuron whose cell body resides in the preanal ganglion.
source: The DA9 neuron is a cholinergic motor neuron whose cell body resides in the preanal ganglion.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text and is established knowledge about DA9 anatomy.

claim: DA9 axon initially extends posteriorly along the ventral nerve cord and through commissure join the dorsal nerve cord where it then extends anteriorly to form en passant synapses onto dorsal body wall muscles.
source: DA9 axon initially extends posteriorly along the ventral nerve cord and through commissure join the dorsal nerve cord where it then extends anteriorly to form en passant synapses onto dorsal body wall muscles (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 6G.

claim: LIN-44/Wnt gradient from the tail hypodermal cells inhibits synapse formation in the posterior axonal region of DA9, creating the synapse-free (or asynaptic) axonal domain.
source: Previous works have shown that LIN-44/Wnt gradient from the tail hypodermal cells inhibits synapse formation in the posterior axonal region of DA9, creating the synapse-free (or asynaptic) axonal domain (Figure 6A and D) (Klassen and Shen, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Klassen and Shen, 2007 and confirmed by data in Figure 6A and D.

claim: In the lin-44 null mutants, ectopic synapse formation occurs in the dorsal posterior axonal domain of DA9.
source: In the lin-44 null mutants, the ectopic synapse formation occurs in the dorsal posterior axonal domain of DA9 (Figure 6B and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B and D.

claim: LIN-17::mCherry is localized within the asynaptic posterior axonal domain in a lin-44-dependent manner.
source: LIN-17::mCherry is localized within the asynaptic posterior axonal domain in a lin-44-dependent manner (Figure 6A and B, middle panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Overexpression of lin-44 from the egl-20 promoter creates a larger asynaptic domain by displacing DA9 synapses more anteriorly.
source: Overexpression of lin-44 from the egl-20 promoter creates a larger asynaptic domain by displacing DA9 synapses more anteriorly, suggesting the LIN-44 gradient determines the length of the asynaptic domain (Klassen and Shen, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Klassen and Shen, 2007.

claim: The LIN-44 gradient determines the length of the asynaptic domain in DA9.
source: Overexpression of lin-44 from the egl-20 promoter creates a larger asynaptic domain by displacing DA9 synapses more anteriorly, suggesting the LIN-44 gradient determines the length of the asynaptic domain (Klassen and Shen, 2007).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the cited work.

claim: The termination of the axonal outgrowth of the DD6 GABAergic motor neuron in the dorsal nerve cord is dependent on the LIN-44 gradient.
source: In addition to the role of LIN-44 gradient in inhibiting synapse formation, the termination of the axonal outgrowth of the DD6 GABAergic motor neuron in the dorsal nerve cord is dependent on the LIN-44 gradient (Maro et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Maro et al., 2009.

claim: In wildtype, the DD6 axon terminates before it reaches the rectum region.
source: In wildtype, the DD6 axon terminates before it reaches the rectum region (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: In lin-44 null mutants, DD6 axon overextends beyond the rectum.
source: In lin-44 null mutants, it overextends beyond the rectum (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: Overexpression of lin-44 from the lin-44 or egl-20 promoters caused premature termination of the DD6 axon outgrowth.
source: Overexpression of lin-44 from the lin-44 or egl-20 promoters caused premature termination of the DD6 axon outgrowth (Maro et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Maro et al., 2009.

claim: The LIN-44 gradient-dependent phenomena (DA9 synapse patterning and DD6 axon termination) were severely disrupted in nrt-bfp-lin-44 animals and were indistinguishable from those in lin-44 null mutants.
source: These two LIN-44 gradient-dependent phenomena were severely disrupted in nrt-bfp-lin-44 animals and were indistinguishable from those in lin-44 null mutants (Figure 6C–6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C-6F.

claim: Membrane-tethered LIN-44 is not capable of exerting the gradient-dependent function of LIN-44.
source: These results strongly suggest that membrane-tethered LIN-44 is not capable of exerting the gradient-dependent function of LIN-44.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing that nrt-bfp-lin-44 cannot rescue gradient-dependent phenotypes.

claim: The position of presynaptic RAB-3 puncta in the PDB neuron is dependent on the LIN-44 gradient.
source: Consistent with this idea, we found that the position of presynaptic RAB-3 puncta in the PDB neuron is dependent on the LIN-44 gradient.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations described in the text.

claim: The PDB neuron has a large asynaptic domain in the dorsal neurite similar to DA9.
source: Similar to DA9, the PDB neuron has a large asynaptic domain in the dorsal neurite (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In both lin-44 null and nrt-bfp-lin-44 animals, ectopic mCherry::RAB-3 puncta were observed in the dorsal neurite of PDB.
source: In both lin-44 null and nrt-bfp-lin-44 animals, we observed ectopic mCherry::RAB-3 puncta in this neurite domain.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations.

claim: PDB can respond to diffusible and non-diffusible Wnt signal in a context-dependent manner.
source: This result suggests that PDB can respond to diffusible and non-diffusible Wnt signal in a context-dependent manner: it utilizes LIN-44 gradient signal to determine its cell fate, neurite guidance and the subcellular localization of the presynaptic vesicles, while its neurite pruning is induced by gradient-independent LIN-44 signal.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the differential effects of membrane-tethered vs. diffusible LIN-44 on different aspects of PDB development.

claim: PDB utilizes LIN-44 gradient signal to determine its cell fate, neurite guidance and the subcellular localization of the presynaptic vesicles.
source: This result suggests that PDB can respond to diffusible and non-diffusible Wnt signal in a context-dependent manner: it utilizes LIN-44 gradient signal to determine its cell fate, neurite guidance and the subcellular localization of the presynaptic vesicles, while its neurite pruning is induced by gradient-independent LIN-44 signal.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing that these processes require diffusible LIN-44.

claim: PDB neurite pruning is induced by gradient-independent LIN-44 signal.
source: This result suggests that PDB can respond to diffusible and non-diffusible Wnt signal in a context-dependent manner: it utilizes LIN-44 gradient signal to determine its cell fate, neurite guidance and the subcellular localization of the presynaptic vesicles, while its neurite pruning is induced by gradient-independent LIN-44 signal.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing that membrane-tethered LIN-44 is sufficient for pruning.

claim: Frizzled receptors are localized to the site of action in Wnt-dependent manners.
source: Wnt ligands activate intracellular signaling cascade by inducing the clustering of the receptors. Consistently, Frizzled receptors are localized to the site of action in Wnt-dependent manners.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Wnt signaling.

claim: LIN-17/Fz is localized asymmetrically on the cell cortex during asymmetric cell division, to the posterior neurite of the PLM mechanosensory neuron during neuronal polarization, and to the posterior asynaptic axonal domain to inhibit presynaptic assembly.
source: For example, LIN-17/Fz is localized asymmetrically on the cell cortex during asymmetric cell division, to the posterior neurite of the PLM mechanosensory neuron during neuronal polarization, and to the posterior asynaptic axonal domain to inhibit presynaptic assembly (Goldstein et al., 2006; Hilliard and Bargmann, 2006; Klassen and Shen, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Significantly higher accumulation of LIN-17::GFP puncta was observed at the tip of the posterior neurites compared with those at the anterior neurite at L2 stage.
source: We observed significantly higher accumulation of LIN-17::GFP puncta at the tip of the posterior neurites compared with those at the anterior neurite at L2 stage (Figure 7A and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7A and D.

claim: The asymmetric LIN-17::GFP localization at the posterior neurites is dependent on lin-44/wnt.
source: The asymmetric LIN-17::GFP localization at the posterior neurites is dependent on lin-44/wnt: we did not observe significant LIN-17::GFP puncta in the lin-44 null mutant animals (Figure 7B and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B and D.

claim: LIN-17::GFP puncta were accumulated at the posterior neurites of PDB in the nrt-bfp-lin-44 animals.
source: In contrast, LIN-17::GFP puncta were accumulated at the posterior neurites of PDB in the nrt-bfp-lin-44 animals (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: The LIN-17::GFP puncta observed in the ventral neurite of wildtype animals were absent in the nrt-bfp-lin-44 animals.
source: We note that the LIN-17::GFP puncta observed in the ventral neurite of wildtype animals were the absent in the nrt-bfp-lin-44 animals (Figure 7A and C).
evidence: The claim is based on observations from Figure 7A and C.

claim: The LIN-17::GFP puncta in the ventral neurite might be associated with the gradient-dependent function of lin-44 such as neuronal polarization and guidance.
source: These LIN-17::GFP puncta might be associated with the gradient-dependent function of lin-44 such as neuronal polarization and guidance.
evidence: The claim is speculation based on the observation that these puncta are absent in nrt-bfp-lin-44.

claim: Dishevelled (Dsh/Dvl) proteins are the intracellular signaling components of both canonical and non-canonical Wnt signaling.
source: Dishevelled (Dsh/Dvl) proteins are the intracellular signaling components of both canonical and non-canonical Wnt signaling and are known to co-localize with active Frizzled receptors (Wallingford and Habas, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wallingford and Habas, 2005.

claim: Dishevelled proteins are known to co-localize with active Frizzled receptors.
source: Dishevelled (Dsh/Dvl) proteins are the intracellular signaling components of both canonical and non-canonical Wnt signaling and are known to co-localize with active Frizzled receptors (Wallingford and Habas, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wallingford and Habas, 2005.

claim: There are three Dishevelled genes in C. elegans (dsh-1, dsh-2 and mig-5).
source: There are three Dishevelled genes in C. elegans (dsh-1, dsh-2 and mig-5).
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans genetics.

claim: Dsh proteins are often localized asymmetrically within the cells in Wnt-dependent manners.

evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: No significant pruning defects were observed in dsh-1 and mig-5 single mutant animals, likely due to their functional redundancy.

claim: DSH-1/Dsh::GFP puncta were localized in the posterior neurites in the wildtype and nrt-bfp-lin-44 but not in the lin-44 null animals.
source: Nevertheless, DSH-1/Dsh::GFP puncta were localized in the posterior neurites in the wildtype and nrt-bfp-lin-44 but not in the lin-44 null animals (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

claim: DSH-1 localization at the posterior neurites was dependent on the LIN-17/Fz receptor.
source: Consistent with the idea that Dsh proteins are recruited to the active Frizzled receptors, DSH-1 localization at the posterior neurites was dependent on the LIN-17/Fz receptor (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Locally restricted Wnt instructs asymmetric neurite pruning via recruiting Frizzled receptor and Dishevelled proteins to the pruning neurites.
source: Taken these results together, we concluded that the locally restricted Wnt instructs asymmetric neurite pruning via recruiting Frizzled receptor and Dishevelled proteins to the pruning neurites (Figure 8).

claim: In C. elegans, two Wnts, CWN-1 and CWN-2, act through CAM-1/Ror to protect neurites from the mbr-1-mediated pruning in the AIM interneurons.
source: In C. elegans, two Wnts, CWN-1 and CWN-2, act through CAM-1/Ror (receptor tyrosine kinase) to protect neurites from the mbr-1-mediated pruning in the AIM interneurons: the pruning defect in AIMs of mbr-1 mutants is suppressed by mutations in cam-1, while overexpression of cam-1 in AIMs inhibits neurite pruning (Hayashi et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hayashi et al., 2009.

claim: CWN-1/2 inhibit neurite pruning in AIMs, in contrast to LIN-44/Wnt which instructs neurite pruning in PDB.

evidence: The claim is an inference based on comparing the effects of different Wnts in different neurons.

claim: cam-1/Ror and lin-17/fz function antagonistically.

claim: Wnt signaling has a conserved role as a pruning cue across species.
source: While it remains to be determined whether Wnt signaling plays an instructive or a permissive role in CSDn dendrite pruning, these observations along with our present study show conserved role of Wnt signaling as a pruning cue.
